zone: Flat Creek and the upper Stehekin valley
_areas_note: Rimrock Ridge alone. THE GROUPING WAS CHECKED AGAINST THE GROUND RATHER THAN TAKEN ON TRUST, and the ridge turns out to be a watershed divide: its north side drains into Flat Creek and its south side into the West Fork of Agnes Creek, with the summit line sitting exactly on the boundary between the two. The Flat Creek side is the approach — a road walk and a maintained valley trail — and that is why this file exists. NOT added to either Ptarmigan crest file: the ridge stands a couple of miles east of the crest, and the traverse camps serve summits above the glaciers on the far side of it. NOT added to the existing Stehekin file either, and that one needed the check: that file's West Fork Agnes bivy is in the same named drainage as this peak's south side, but it sits at the far eastern end of it under Agnes Mountain, more than ten kilometres away up a drainage whose trail has all but vanished, so it is not a base for this summit. The landing camps and the shuttle terminus at High Bridge are recorded in that file and are NOT duplicated here even though every party passes through both; Bridge Creek camps are left out because a neighbouring file already holds them. What is here is the upper-valley road camps above the shuttle's end, the camp at the Flat Creek trailhead, and the trailless ground beyond the end of that trail.

sites.name: Dolly Varden Camp, upper Stehekin valley road
sites.capacity: Small designated camp beside the old road, a handful of sites in forest by the river. Assigned by night on the permit.
sites.water: The Stehekin River is immediately there and runs all season. Treat it — it is a big glacial river and carries silt as well as everything else in the drainage.
sites.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, covering Lake Chelan National Recreation Area as well as the park proper. Obtained at the Golden West visitor centre at the landing on arrival, or at Marblemount if you are coming over a pass. THE PERMIT AND THE BOAT HAVE TO AGREE: an itinerary that slips a day because you missed a sailing needs the permit amended, and the office that can do that is back at the landing.
sites.notes: About thirteen miles up from the landing, which puts it roughly two above the shuttle's turnaround at High Bridge. Its whole purpose on this trip is to absorb the arrival day. The boat gets in around the middle of the day, the last shuttle up the valley leaves in the late afternoon, and nobody sensibly starts a twenty-mile approach on that schedule — so you ride to High Bridge, walk a short way, and sleep. It is flat forest with no view and no alpine character at all, which is exactly what it is for. NOTE ANOTHER CLOSURE NEARBY: the camp at Tumwater, at around two thousand feet a little further down the same stretch of road, has been shut after high water damaged it, and the park asked people to stay away from the valley altogether after a bad flood. Between that and the fire seasons, confirm which upper-valley camps are actually open before you build the itinerary, because there are not many of them and losing one changes the whole plan.

sites.name: Flat Creek Camp, at the trailhead
sites.capacity: A physically large camp that nonetheless takes only about two large groups, so it is emptier than it looks and still bookable out. Stock parties use it as well as walkers.
sites.water: Flat Creek runs at the camp and the Stehekin River is close by. Both are reliable through the climbing season.
sites.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit, same system as the rest of the valley. This camp sits inside the park; the ground you climb on does not. See the note below on where the boundary falls, because the two agencies want different things and the changeover happens two miles up the trail.
sites.notes: THIS IS THE CAMP FOR THE PEAK. It sits where the Flat Creek trail leaves the old valley road, about nine and a half miles above High Bridge on what used to be driveable and has been a walking route since the river took the road out for the last time more than two decades ago. That distance is the real cost of this objective: the public shuttle stops at High Bridge and everything above it is on foot, so from the boat you are looking at twenty miles of approach before the climbing starts. From here the Flat Creek trail runs four miles or so up the valley on gentle ground, gaining only a few hundred feet, through old growth and through forest still recovering from a fire early this century. It ends well short of the head of the valley, and Rimrock Ridge is beyond where it ends.

sites.name: Cottonwood Camp, end of the road
sites.capacity: The largest camp in the upper valley, big enough to take groups and long used as a staging point for parties crossing Park Creek Pass or coming over Cascade Pass. Still permit-assigned by night.
sites.water: River and tributary water at the camp, reliable all season and needing treatment like everything else in the drainage.
sites.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required. Book or claim the nights in the same transaction as the rest of the itinerary; a party walking this far does not want to discover a gap in the middle of it.
sites.notes: Twenty-three miles from the landing at the very end of the old road, something under four miles past the Flat Creek junction. It is included because it is the upper valley's anchor camp and the obvious fallback if Flat Creek Camp is taken, at the cost of walking past your turning and back. It also marks where the OTHER approaches join: parties come down to here over Park Creek Pass from the Thunder Creek side, and over Cascade Pass from the Cascade River road, which reaches the Flat Creek junction in something over thirteen miles. Either is a genuine alternative to the boat, and both are long. No elevation is recorded because no confident figure was found for the camp itself.

sites.name: Bivouacs in the upper Flat Creek basin, beyond the end of the trail
sites.capacity: No established camping and no site count. THERE IS NOTHING UP HERE. The trail stops, and a party going on picks whatever flat gravel, slab or old moraine it can find in the head of the valley. Anyone describing a camp here is describing a place they happened to sleep.
sites.water: Creek and snowmelt throughout the basin, which is at least the easy part — this is a wet north-facing valley fed off the glaciers on the crest above it, and running water is not the problem here that it is on a ridge camp.
sites.permit: THE AGENCY CHANGES ON THIS TRAIL, and it is the thing most likely to be got wrong. The Flat Creek trail leaves the national park about two miles up and passes into the Glacier Peak Wilderness under the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, so the ground you actually camp and climb on is Forest Service. Checked against the boundary rather than assumed: the summit itself lies inside the Glacier Peak Wilderness. That means a free self-issue wilderness permit rather than a paid park permit, no reservation, and a party limit of TWELVE counting people and pack animals together — larger than the park's six, and a rare case where walking further gets you a looser rule. Groups over twelve must split and stay a mile apart. The park permit still covers the valley camps you slept in getting there, so a full trip needs both. There is NO named park cross-country zone for Flat Creek — that is not a gap in the record, the zone system simply does not reach here, because the ground is not the park's. Standard wilderness practice applies: durable surfaces, well back from the water, pack out what will not bury.
sites.notes: Rimrock Ridge is an obscure summit and should be described as one. It forms the southern rim of the upper Flat Creek valley — everything falling off its far side goes into the West Fork of Agnes Creek instead — and it looks across at the glaciated back of the crest that the classic traverse walks along. Accounts of that traverse do not mention it, because climbers up there are facing the other way, and no ascent account of it was found at all. The approach is the whole difficulty: boat, shuttle, most of a day walking the old road, a gentle valley trail, and then trailless ground up the headwaters to whatever line goes. Expect brush low down and then open country once the timber releases. Budget four days minimum for a trip that would be an afternoon if a road came anywhere near it, and build the itinerary around the boat timetable rather than around the climbing, because a missed sailing costs a whole day at each end. Late summer into early autumn is the window: the valley approach is snow-free long before the head of it is, and the same fire and flood seasons that have been closing camps in this valley can close the trail as well.
